q: What internal temperature makes cooked chicken safe to eat?
why: 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part kills the bacteria that cause food poisoning. Use a thermometer, not colour.

q: What is the safe internal temperature for ground beef?
why: Grinding mixes surface bacteria all the way through, so ground meat needs 160°F (71°C).

q: Whole cuts of beef or pork, like steaks and chops, are safe at what temperature, followed by a short rest?
why: 145°F (63°C), then rest 3 minutes. The rest finishes the job and keeps the juices in.

q: Fish is cooked through at what internal temperature?
why: 145°F (63°C), when the flesh turns opaque and flakes easily.

q: Bacteria grow fastest between which temperatures, called the danger zone?
why: Between 40°F (4°C) and 140°F (60°C) bacteria multiply quickly. Keep cold food cold and hot food hot.

q: How soon should cooked food go in the fridge?
why: Within 2 hours (1 hour if it is hotter than 90°F outside). After that, bacteria have had too long to grow.

q: How long do cooked leftovers keep in the fridge?
why: 3 to 4 days. After that, throw them out, even if they look and smell fine.

q: Should you rinse raw chicken before cooking it?
options: No, it spreads germs around the sink
why: Rinsing splashes raw-chicken bacteria onto the sink and counters. Cooking to 165°F is what makes it safe.

q: What is the best way to avoid cross-contamination?
options: Use the same board and wash it once at the end
Use separate boards (or wash well) for raw meat and ready-to-eat food
Rinse the knife with cold water
why: Raw meat juices can carry bacteria. Keep a separate board, or wash the board, knife and your hands before touching anything that won't be cooked.

q: How long should you wash your hands with soap before cooking?
why: At least 20 seconds, about two rounds of the happy birthday song, then dry them on a clean towel.

q: What is the safest way to thaw frozen meat?
options: In a bowl of hot water
why: The fridge keeps it out of the danger zone. Cold running water or the microwave also work if you cook it right away.

q: What temperature should your fridge be at or below?
why: 40°F (4°C) or colder slows bacteria. The freezer should be 0°F (-18°C).

q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
options: It cuts faster so you finish sooner
It needs less force, so it is less likely to slip
why: A dull knife needs more force and skids off the food. A sharp one goes where you point it.

q: What is the "claw grip" for the hand holding the food?
options: Fingers curled under, knuckles guide the blade
Fingers flat on top of the food
Holding the food in the air
why: Curling your fingertips under keeps them out of the way while your knuckles guide the side of the blade.

q: Which knife cuts a ripe tomato cleanly without squashing it?
options: A serrated (bread) knife or very sharp knife
why: A serrated knife saws through the tough skin without pressing the soft inside.

q: Which cut is the smallest?
why: Mincing makes tiny pieces, usually for garlic, ginger and herbs.

q: What does "julienne" mean?
why: Julienne cuts are thin, even matchsticks, about the size of a match.

q: What does "sauté" mean?
options: Cook slowly in lots of water
Cook quickly in a little fat over fairly high heat
why: Sauté means quick cooking in a small amount of fat, moving the food around in the pan.

q: What does it mean to "sear" meat?
options: Brown the surface over high heat
why: Searing browns the outside over high heat, which builds a lot of flavor.

q: What does a simmer look like?
options: Big rolling bubbles and lots of steam
why: A simmer has small, gentle bubbles. A boil is large and rolling.

q: What is blanching?
options: Boiling briefly, then cooling in ice water
why: Blanching quickly cooks vegetables and the ice bath stops the cooking, keeping them bright and crisp.

q: What does "deglaze" mean?
options: Add liquid to loosen the browned bits stuck to the pan
Take the glaze off a cake
why: Browned bits in the pan are flavor. A splash of broth, wine or water dissolves them into your sauce.

q: What does "fold" mean when baking?
options: Gently combine so you keep the air in
Stir in circles for a minute
why: Folding uses a spatula to lift and turn the mixture gently so it stays light and airy.

q: Why let cooked meat rest before cutting?
options: So it cools to a safe temperature
So the juices settle back into the meat
why: Cutting right away lets the juices run out. A few minutes' rest keeps the meat moist.

q: Why should you not overcrowd the pan?
why: Too much food releases too much steam. Cook in batches so the food can brown.

q: Why preheat the pan before adding food?
options: Food sears and is less likely to stick
It is only needed for baking
why: A hot pan browns food right away. Cold food in a cold pan tends to stick and turn grey.

q: Why salt the pasta water?
options: It seasons the pasta as it cooks
why: Salted water seasons the pasta from the inside. It should taste like mild sea water.

q: What does "al dente" mean?
why: Al dente is Italian for "to the tooth": cooked through but still a little firm.

q: What does baking soda need in a recipe to work?
options: An acid such as buttermilk, yogurt or lemon
why: Baking soda reacts with acid to make bubbles. Baking powder already includes its own acid.

q: What is the best way to measure flour with cups?
options: Scoop it straight from the bag and press
Spoon it into the cup and level the top
why: Scooping packs the flour and you end up with too much. Spoon it in and level it, or better, weigh it.

q: How many teaspoons are in a tablespoon?
why: 1 tablespoon = 3 teaspoons.

q: How many tablespoons are in a cup?
why: 1 cup = 16 tablespoons (and 8 fluid ounces).

q: What is "mise en place"?
options: Having everything prepped and in place before you start cooking
why: It means "everything in its place": chop, measure and set out before the heat goes on, so nothing burns while you hunt for the salt.

q: How can you tell oil is hot enough to cook with?
options: It shimmers and flows easily in the pan
It is cold to the touch
why: Hot oil shimmers and spreads easily. If it is smoking, it is too hot: turn it down.

q: A pan of oil catches fire. What should you do?
options: Cover it with a lid and turn off the heat
why: Smother it with a lid or baking sheet and turn off the heat. Water makes a grease fire explode.

q: What should never go in the microwave?
options: Metal foil or a metal pan
why: Metal can spark and damage the microwave. Use microwave-safe glass or ceramic.

q: Which way should pot handles point while cooking?
options: Over the front of the stove
why: Turning handles inward keeps you from bumping a pot and pulling it off the stove.

q: How should you care for a cast iron pan?
options: Soak it overnight in soapy water
Wash it, dry it right away and wipe on a thin layer of oil
why: Dry it fully and wipe on a little oil. Soaking and the dishwasher cause rust.

q: What should you avoid using on a nonstick pan?
why: Metal scratches the coating. Use wood, silicone or heat-safe plastic.

q: How can you test if an egg is fresh?
options: It sinks and lies flat in water
why: Fresh eggs sink and lie flat. As air builds inside, older eggs stand up or float.

q: Why put hard-boiled eggs in ice water?
options: It stops the cooking and makes them easier to peel
It keeps the shell from cracking later
why: The ice bath stops the cooking so the yolk does not turn green, and the egg shrinks slightly from the shell.

q: Why rinse white rice before cooking?
options: To wash off extra surface starch so it is less sticky
why: Rinsing removes loose starch, which gives you fluffier, separate grains.

q: Where should ripe tomatoes be stored for the best flavor?
why: The fridge dulls their flavor and makes them mealy. Keep ripe tomatoes on the counter and use them within a few days.

q: Where do potatoes keep best?
options: In a cool, dark, dry place
why: Light turns potatoes green and the fridge turns their starch to sugar. Keep them cool, dark and dry.

q: Which gas from ripe bananas makes other fruit ripen faster?
why: Ethylene speeds ripening. Keep bananas away from fruit you want to last.

q: Which has the highest smoke point, so it is best for very hot cooking?
why: Refined avocado oil handles very high heat (around 500°F). Butter and flaxseed oil burn much sooner.

q: Where should you marinate raw chicken?
why: Marinate in the fridge so the chicken stays out of the danger zone.

q: A marinade had raw meat in it. How can you use it as a sauce?
options: Pour it straight on the food
Boil it for a few minutes first
why: Raw-meat juices carry bacteria. Bring the marinade to a full boil first, or set aside a separate portion before marinating.

q: Where should you put the thermometer to check meat?
options: In the thickest part, away from bone
why: The thickest part is the last to cook. Bone and fat read differently.

q: What is carryover cooking?
options: Food keeps cooking from its own heat after you take it off the heat
why: A roast or steak can rise 5 to 10°F after it comes off the heat, so pull it a little early.

q: A basic roux is made from what?
why: A roux is fat and flour cooked together, then used to thicken sauces and gravies.

q: A squeeze of lemon juice or a splash of vinegar at the end of a dish does what?
why: A little acid wakes up flavors, especially in rich or heavy dishes.

q: Why add a pinch of salt to sweet baking?
options: To bring out the sweetness and flavor
why: Salt sharpens flavor and balances sweetness, so cookies taste more like cookies.

q: When zesting a lemon, which part do you want?
why: The colored peel holds the fragrant oil. The white pith underneath is bitter.

q: Why add garlic later or cook it on lower heat?
options: It burns quickly and turns bitter
why: Minced garlic browns in under a minute and burnt garlic tastes bitter. Add it near the end or keep the heat moderate.

q: Why save a cup of starchy pasta water?
options: To help the sauce cling and become silky
why: The starch in the water thickens and binds the sauce so it coats the pasta.

q: How long can raw chicken stay in the fridge before cooking or freezing?
why: Cook or freeze raw chicken within 1 to 2 days of buying it.

q: Why does cutting onions make your eyes water?
options: They release an irritating gas when the cells break
It is the smell of the oil
why: Cutting breaks cells and sets off a reaction that makes a gas that stings your eyes. A sharp knife breaks fewer cells.

q: How should you cool a big pot of soup before storing it?
options: Leave it on the stove overnight
Split it into shallow containers so it cools quickly
Put the whole hot pot in the fridge
why: Shallow containers cool fast, so the soup spends less time in the danger zone.

q: Which is the best way to slice a round vegetable such as an onion or potato safely?
options: Hold it in the air and cut toward your hand
Cut a flat side first so it sits steady on the board
why: A flat side gives you a stable base so the food cannot roll while you cut.

q: A damp towel under the cutting board does what?
why: A damp towel or non-slip mat grips the counter so the board stays put.

q: Why should you taste as you cook?
options: To check whether the pan is hot
why: Tasting along the way lets you add salt, acid or spice a little at a time instead of fixing it at the end.
